title: Polynomial-time recognition of abelian cores
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite algebra \(\mathbf A\) by full tables of its basic operations and promised that \(\mathbf A\) has an idempotent Taylor term, decides whether the core of \(\mathbf A\) is abelian? This selects the decision part of Theorem 3, whose quasipolynomial running time is the subject of the source’s open question.

source_formulation.text: We do not know whether the quasi-polynomial time algorithms in Theorem 3 can be improved to polynomial time.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 5

context:
Theorem 3 decides abelianness of the core for every finite algebra in a Taylor variety. In positive cases it also computes the core and the table of its Mal’cev term operation. The open continuation asks whether the quasipolynomial algorithms can be made polynomial. The present card isolates recognition as one precise component.

Under the stronger congruence-modular assumption, Theorem 2 identifies abelian cores as the tractable side of the dichotomy for systems of term equations over a fixed algebra; the other side is NP-complete. This explains the recognition problem’s motivation. Theorem 3 itself has the broader Taylor promise, so that stronger assumption must not be substituted into its input specification.

The source notes that testing for a Taylor term on an arbitrary finite operation-table algebra is EXPTIME-complete. Here its existence is promised. Conversely, the not-necessarily-idempotent Taylor polymorphism used elsewhere in the paper’s general CSP dichotomy is a different notion from the idempotent Taylor term in this promise.

Aichinger’s June 2024 lecture on equations over finite algebras restates Mayr’s quasipolynomial recognition bound when discussing the congruence-modular case. It distinguishes the problem of classifying a supplied algebra from solving equations over a fixed one.
why: Measures the cost of recognizing algebraic structure that can make entire families of equation systems tractable. The question asks whether a useful structural classification can be found with polynomial preprocessing, rather than only being available as a theorem about each fixed algebra.
status_note: Read the complete original question, Theorems 1–3, core and Taylor definitions, the matrix definition of abelianness, and Section 5’s quasipolynomial bound. Read the June 2024 overview’s meta-problem discussion. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no polynomial-time improvement for the stated promise problem. The decision branch is explicitly selected; no equivalence with the additional constructive outputs or with unrestricted equation solving is assumed.

sentences: The input is an entire finite algebra specified by tables of its basic operations.
It is promised to possess an idempotent Taylor term, although no witness is supplied.
The task is to decide whether its smallest endomorphic image is abelian in the universal-algebraic sense.
A quasipolynomial-time recognition algorithm is known.
This is a classification problem for algebras, distinct from solving a particular list of term equations.

definitions:
A finite algebra \(\mathbf A=(A;f_{1},\ldots,f_{m})\) has a nonempty explicitly listed finite universe and a finite signature. Each basic operation \(f_{j}:A^{r_{j}}\to A\) is supplied by its complete table, with its arity. Nullary operations, when present, specify distinguished constants. The universe size, number of operations and arities may vary with the input. Let \(L\) be the total binary length of this description. A large-arity operation is not given by a succinct circuit or program.

A term is an expression made from variables and the given operation symbols; interpreting it on \(\mathbf A\) gives a term operation. Constants not in the given signature are not automatically available as term symbols.

The Taylor promise means that there are an arity \(r\geq2\) and a term operation \(t:A^{r}\to A\) such that \(t(a,\ldots,a)=a\) for every \(a\in A\), and for every coordinate \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) there are two tuples \(\mathbf u_{i},\mathbf v_{i}\in\{x,y\}^{r}\) with \((\mathbf u_{i})_{i}=x\), \((\mathbf v_{i})_{i}=y\), satisfying
\[t(\mathbf u_{i}(a,b))=t(\mathbf v_{i}(a,b))\qquad\text{for every }a,b\in A.\]
The choices of \(r,t\) and identities may depend on the algebra. This is what the source means by membership in a Taylor variety. A witnessing term or operation table is not supplied, and recognizing whether the promise holds is not part of the task.

An endomorphism of \(\mathbf A\) is a map \(h:A\to A\) preserving every basic operation:
\[h(f_{j}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{r_{j}}))=f_{j}(h(a_{1}),\ldots,h(a_{r_{j}})).\]
It must also fix the interpretation of every nullary symbol. Its image is a subalgebra. A core is an endomorphic image minimal under inclusion among such images, equipped with the restricted operations. For finite algebras these cores are unique up to isomorphism; equivalently, every endomorphism of the core is an automorphism.

Abelianness here is the universal-algebraic term-condition property. A concrete definition uses the algebra of \(2\times2\) matrices over a finite algebra \(\mathbf B\), with each basic operation applied entrywise. Let \(M_{\mathbf B}\) be the smallest subset of \(B^{2\times2}\) closed under these operations and containing all matrices
\[\begin{pmatrix}a&a\\ b&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}c&d\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\qquad(a,b,c,d\in B).\]
Then \(\mathbf B\) is abelian if every matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}x&y\\ z&w\end{pmatrix}\in M_{\mathbf B}\) satisfies \(x=y\Rightarrow z=w\). This is the source’s condition \([1_{\mathbf B},1_{\mathbf B}]=0_{\mathbf B}\). It is not a requirement that each basic operation be commutative.

One uniform deterministic algorithm must run in \(O(L^{k})\) bit operations for a fixed constant \(k\), with a fixed multiplicative constant, on all inputs. It must answer correctly for every well-formed algebra satisfying the Taylor promise. On other inputs the answer is unrestricted, but the polynomial time bound still applies. The requested output is only YES or NO; no particular representative of the core has to be chosen.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm with a uniform polynomial bound in the full table encoding length that recognizes abelian cores on every promised input, or prove that none exists. A conditional lower bound must identify its assumption. The source also asks for faster construction of the core and its Mal’cev operation in positive cases; those are additional output tasks and are not silently asserted equivalent to the selected decision question.
